intro: Chinese characters don't spell out their own pronunciation the way an alphabet does, so this is a sound reference rather than a character reference — a key to the IPA you'll see throughout this vocabulary. Two things trip up English speakers in particular: tones aren't just pitch levels, most of them are moving contours (see Tones below, shown as a small colored line over the syllable, not a number), and Mandarin's stop/affricate consonants aren't organized by voicing like English b/p or d/t — almost all of them come in unaspirated/aspirated pairs instead (whether there's a puff of air or not), which matters more here than voicing does. These are IPA symbols, not pinyin letters — if you already know pinyin, note the letters don't carry over directly (pinyin 'b' is IPA [p], pinyin 'p' is IPA [pʰ], and so on).

items.note: 1st tone — level and high, stays flat for the whole syllable
2nd tone — rising, starts mid and climbs to high
3rd tone — dipping, starts low-ish, drops to the bottom, then rises
4th tone — falling, starts at the top and drops sharply
neutral tone — a small gray dot instead of a colored line; short, light, and toneless, and always attaches to the syllable before it
unaspirated — no puff of air, like the p in English "spin"
aspirated — a real puff of air, like the p in English "pin"
